text: {"answer": "Nuclear power is a low-carbon source and can help cut emissions, but its cost-effectiveness and speed of deployment are contested. Supporting evidence says nuclear plants emit no greenhouse gases during operation and have life-cycle emissions similar to wind and about a third of solar's per unit of electricity [8ef6c9360938#3]. The IAEA reports that nuclear output, alongside renewables and fuel switching, helped level global CO2 emissions in 2019 [7e88e103d8fb#0]. Experts quoted by the World Nuclear Association argue that deep decarbonization to limit warming to 1.5°C would be much harder without a larger nuclear role [8ef6c9360938#3]. The contradicting evidence is substantial. A Boston University study finds nuclear plants carry the highest construction risk, with an average cost overrun of 102.5% and the most extreme delays [06384d0fb532#2], while solar projects have the best track record [06384d0fb532#3]. A cost study notes nuclear has grown more expensive while renewables have fallen in cost [3f84053483c2#0], and an arXiv model of Sweden finds little cost benefit from reinvesting in nuclear [6b0ccdbcf9aa#1]. Overall, nuclear cuts carbon, but cost and delay risks weaken its case against renewables.", "confidence": 60, "one_line": "Nuclear is low-carbon and helps decarbonize, but high construction costs and delays make it a debated choice versus renewables."}
